subject: Medicine
summary: Hyperkalaemia is an elevated serum potassium level that can cause life‑threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Diagnosis relies on lab values and ECG changes, and treatment must act quickly to protect the heart and lower potassium.

sections.p: Hyperkalaemia is defined as serum potassium >5.0 mmol/L. Diagnosis requires a reliable potassium measurement and assessment for ECG abnormalities.
b: Serum K+ >5.0 mmol/L confirms the diagnosis
ECG changes guide urgency of treatment

sections.p: Severity guides management urgency and choice of interventions.
b: Mild: 5.1‑5.9 mmol/L, usually no ECG changes
Moderate: 6.0‑6.4 mmol/L, may show peaked T waves
Severe: ≥6.5 mmol/L or any ECG abnormality, high risk of arrhythmia

sections.p: Identify the underlying driver to stop further potassium rise.
b: Renal failure (acute or chronic) – most common
Potassium‑sparing drugs (spironolactone, ACE‑I, ARB, NSAIDs)
Cellular shift (acidosis, insulin deficiency, β‑blocker overdose)
Massive tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, burns)
Tropical infections causing renal injury (malaria, severe dengue, schistosomiasis)
Herbal remedies high in potassium

sections.p: Symptoms are often nonspecific; cardiac signs dominate.
b: Muscle weakness or paresthesia
Palpitations, chest discomfort
Nausea, vomiting
ECG: peaked T waves → widened QRS → sine‑wave pattern

sections.p: Tests must answer why potassium is high and whether the heart is affected.

t.b: What is the exact potassium level? Guides severity staging
Are there arrhythmic changes? Determines need for immediate calcium
Is the kidney unable to excrete potassium? Directs removal strategy
Is there metabolic acidosis causing a shift? Helps decide shift therapy
Which drugs could be raising potassium? Guides cessation

sections.p: Rapidly rising potassium can cause fatal arrhythmias.
b: ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS, sine wave)
Sudden cardiac arrest
Severe metabolic acidosis

sections.p: Treat the heart first, then shift potassium intracellularly, and finally remove excess.
b: IV calcium gluconate if ECG changes – stabilises myocardial membrane
Insulin + dextrose (or IV glucose) – drives K+ into cells
Nebulised salbutamol – β2 agonist shift without glucose load
Loop diuretic (if urine output) – promotes renal excretion
Sodium bicarbonate if severe acidosis – shifts K+ and corrects pH
Dialysis for refractory or renal failure cases – definitive removal

sections.p: Prevent recurrence by addressing chronic causes and monitoring.
b: Regular potassium checks in CKD or on potassium‑sparing drugs
Educate patients on low‑potassium diet and avoiding herbal supplements
Adjust or stop offending medications

sections.p: Conditions that mimic ECG or symptom patterns.
b: Hypokalaemia – can also cause arrhythmias but shows flattened T waves
Hypercalcaemia – may cause shortened QT, not peaked T
Hemolysed blood sample falsely raises potassium – repeat if suspicion
Delayed ECG after treatment may still show changes despite safe potassium

whenToSeekHelp: New or worsening chest pain, syncope, or palpitations with any ECG abnormality
Severe muscle weakness progressing to paralysis
Rapid rise in potassium (>6.5 mmol/L) on repeat testing

faq.a: Calcium stabilises cardiac membranes immediately, while insulin works slower to shift potassium.

faq.q: Can oral potassium binders be used in emergencies?
faq.a: They act over hours and are not suitable for acute life‑threatening hyperkalaemia.
Maximise diuretics, give repeated insulin/dextrose, and consider sodium polystyrene sulfonate if safe.

exam: Explain the stepwise management of severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes.
List the most common causes of hyperkalaemia in a low‑resource setting and how they differ from high‑income settings.
Interpret a sample ECG showing peaked T waves and describe the immediate treatment.
